'''Andre Bernard Tippett Sr.''' (born December 27, 1959) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 11 seasons with the [[New England Patriots]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Iowa Hawkeyes football|Iowa Hawkeyes]], where he was recognized as a consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] in 1981. A second-round pick in the [[1982 NFL draft]], Tippett was selected to five [[Pro Bowl]]s and was named first-team [[All-Pro]] twice in his career. Since 2007, he has been the Patriots' executive director of community affairs.<ref>{{cite web |title=Andre Tippett's LinkedIn |publisher=LinkedIn |date=2022-08-20 |url=https://www.linkedin.com/in/andretippett |access-date=2022-08-20}}</ref> He was enshrined in the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2008.

==Early life==
Tippett was born in [[Birmingham, Alabama]].  He attended [[Barringer High School]] in [[Newark, New Jersey|Newark]], [[New Jersey]].<ref>[http://infoweb.newsbank.com/iw-search/we/InfoWeb?p_action=doc&p_docid=0EFD502D5C99C190&p_docnum=2&p_queryname=NaN&p_product=NewsBank&p_theme=aggregated4&p_nbid=J4BH4EDFMTE4NTg0NzQ0OS4yODY4NjU6MTo3OnJhLTE4ODg "THE ULTIMATE NEW JERSEY HIGH SCHOOL YEARBOOK: T-Z AND ALSO..."], ''[[The Star-Ledger]]'', June 27, 1999. Accessed August 4, 2007.</ref> He first attended college and played football at [[Ellsworth Community College]] in Iowa Falls in 1978.

==College career==
Tippett was an [[1981 College Football All-America Team|All-American]] defensive end and a three-year letterman at the [[University of Iowa]]. He was also a two-time [[List of All-Big Ten Conference football teams|All-Big Ten]] selection (1980 and 1981). In 1981, he helped lead the [[Iowa Hawkeyes football|Hawkeyes]] to their first winning season, their first Big Ten title, and first [[Rose Bowl Game|Rose Bowl]] in two decades. He was part of a defense that allowed only 129 points, the lowest total since 1965 and 9th-best in school history and allowed only 86.9 rushing yards a game, which still stands as the school record. The 1981 Iowa defense allowed 253 total yards a game, the fewest since 1959, making it the 4th-best defense in school history in terms of total yards. Against [[Northwestern University|Northwestern]] on October 3, 1981, the Hawkeye defense allowed 78 total yards which stands as 6th-best in defensive performances in team history.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://graphics.fansonly.com/photos/schools/iowa/sports/m-footbl/auto_pdf/supplement.pdf |title=2007 University of Iowa Football Media Guide |date=July 22, 2008|access-date=November 28, 2008| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20081209174407/http://graphics.fansonly.com/photos/schools/iowa/sports/m-footbl/auto_pdf/supplement.pdf| archive-date= December 9, 2008 | url-status= live}}</ref>

Tippett was a two-time first-team all-Big Ten, and a team captain in 1981. He holds the Iowa record for tackles for lost yardage in a season (20 tackles for 153 yards in 1980).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://graphics.fansonly.com/photos/schools/iowa/sports/m-footbl/auto_pdf/supplement.pdf |title=2007 University of Iowa Football Media Guide |date=July 22, 2008 |access-date=November 28, 2008| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20081209174407/http://graphics.fansonly.com/photos/schools/iowa/sports/m-footbl/auto_pdf/supplement.pdf| archive-date= December 9, 2008 | url-status= live}}</ref> He played in the [[Hula Bowl]] and the Japan Bowl in 1982, after his senior year at Iowa. He was voted a DE on Iowa's all-time football team in 1989 as is a member of the University of Iowa's Varsity Hall of Fame. Upon induction to the Varsity Hall of Fame, Tippett remarked, "For me, this is a 'Wow' . . . It is really, really special to be voted by your peers and the people who saw you play. I'm going in with some of the greatest people to ever play sports at the University of Iowa. This is one of the greatest honors I have ever had. This is a special feeling because during the three years I was there, I developed a great bond with the players and coaches."
<ref>{{cite web |url=http://hawkeyesports.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/090707aaf.html |title=Fry's confidence in Tippett pays big dividends |work=Hawkeyesports.cstv.com |date=August 7, 2007 |access-date=November 28, 2008 |archive-date=June 19, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080619145310/http://hawkeyesports.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/090707aaf.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Professional career==
{{Cquote|[[Lawrence Taylor|L. T.]]'s in a class all by himself. I'll put L. T. first, then Tippett, and [[Cornelius Bennett|Bennett]] behind him.|15px|15px|[[New York Jets|Jets]] [[Fullback (American football)|fullback]] [[Roger Vick]], ranking the [[National Football League|NFL]]'s best pass rushers during the [[1988 NFL season|1988 season]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Eskenazi |first=Gerald |date=October 17, 1988 |title=Bills' Bennett Says He's Best |newspaper=New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/10/17/sports/bills-bennett-says-he-s-best.html }}</ref>}}

Tippett was selected by the New England Patriots in the 2nd round of the [[1982 NFL draft]] with the 41st overall pick.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1982 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1982/draft.htm |access-date=2024-09-13 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

Tippett is a member of the NFL's 1980s all-decade team and was selected to five [[Pro Bowl]]s in his career, earning the nod in five straight seasons from 1984 to 1988.

From 1984 to 1985, Tippett recorded the highest two-season [[sack (football)|sack]] total by a linebacker in NFL history, totaling 35.0 sacks during the two seasons. His 18.5 sacks in 1984 are the third most by any linebacker in a single season, while his 16.5 sacks in 1985 are tied for the sixth most by any linebacker in NFL history.

Tippett holds the Patriots' franchise record with 100.0 career sacks. He also owns the top three single-season sack performances in Patriots history (18.5 in 1984, 16.5 in 1985 and 12.5 in 1987).
He ranked seventh on the all-time sacks list, and third among linebackers, at the time of his retirement following the 1993 season. Over his career, Tippett recorded 100 sacks in 151 games, an average of 0.662 sacks per game. The mark currently ranks fourth in NFL history among linebackers.

After not recording a sack as a rookie in 1982, Tippett finished either first or second on the team in sacks in each of his final 10 seasons. He led the team in sacks six times and finished second on the team four times. Tippett recorded 30 multiple-sack games in his career and sacked a total of 41 different quarterbacks. Tippett recovered 18 opponents' fumbles during his career, tying him for first on the Patriots' all-time list (Steve Nelson). He also forced 17 fumbles in his career.

Tippett was named the AFC's Linebacker of the Year by the [[NFL Players Association]] for three straight seasons from 1985 to 1987. He was voted to the [[Associated Press]] All-NFL First-team on two occasions (1985 and 1987) and Second-team on two other occasions (1986 and 1988). He was also named to the [[NFL Films]] All-Pro team in 1984.

He was voted the [[Newspaper Enterprise Association]] (NEA) co-Defensive Player of the Year (with [[Los Angeles Raiders|Raider]] [[Howie Long]]) in 1985. Additionally, he was voted the 1985 [[UPI AFL-AFC Player of the Year|UPI AFL-AFC Defensive Player of the Year]].

Tippett twice earned AFC Defensive Player of the Week awards.  The first in the Patriots 20–13 win over the New York Jets as he stopped the Jets 3 times within the 10 yard line on 10–20–85. Next, he was the AFC Defensive Player of the Week in the Patriots 21–7 win over the Houston Oilers on October 18, 1987.  In this victory over Houston at the Astrodome, Andre had 3 sacks, defended on a pass play and blocked a field goal attempt that was returned for a touchdown by Raymond Clayborn. He had 1.5 sacks in his final game on January 2, 1994, against the [[Miami Dolphins]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199401020nwe.htm|title=Miami Dolphins at New England Patriots - January 2nd, 1994|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref>

Tippett spent his entire 11-year career with the Patriots and was a member of three playoff teams, including the 1985 AFC Champions.

==Honors==
Tippett was selected to the Patriots' 35th Anniversary Team in 1994 and was selected to the Patriots Team of the Century in 2000. He was inducted into the New England Patriots Hall of Fame in 1999.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.patriots.com/history/index.cfm?ac=halloffameplayer&bio=2174|title=56 Andre Tippett LB|work=Patriots Official website|access-date=November 28, 2008|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091115014830/http://www.patriots.com/history/index.cfm?ac=halloffameplayer&bio=2174|archive-date=November 15, 2009}}</ref> Tippett was inducted into the University of Iowa Hall of Fame on September 7, 2007.

In January 2008, he was voted by a panel of former NFL players and coaches to ''Pro Football Weekly''{{'s}} All-Time 3–4 defensive team along with [[Harry Carson]], [[Lawrence Taylor]], [[Randy Gradishar]], [[Howie Long]], [[Lee Roy Selmon]], and [[Curley Culp]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.profootballweekly.com/PFW/PFW+Online/Volume+22+-+2007/Issue29_view.htm |title=Pro Football Weekly, Volume 22 Issue 29 |work=Profootballweekly.com |date=January 21, 2008 |access-date=November 28, 2008 }}{{dead link|date=December 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

He was named as one of 17 finalists for the Pro Football Hall of Fame's Class of 2007 and 2008.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/sports/football/nfl/2008-01-15-hall-of-fame-finalists_N.htm |title=Cris Carter, Darrell Green finalists for Hall of Fame|work=USA Today website |date=January 15, 2008 |access-date=November 28, 2008}}</ref> As a finalist, he joined other modern-era players and two players selected by the Hall of Fame's Senior Committee in the pool from which the Hall of Fame class was selected.

The Hall of Fame's 40-member Selection Committee met in Miami on February 3, 2007, to select the Class of 2007. Tippett was not selected for enshrinement, but he was among the top 10 finalists. The 44-member Selection Committee met in Arizona, the day prior to Super Bowl XLII, to vote on the Class of 2008. Just prior, Hall of Fame running back [[Eric Dickerson]] said, "I think it is about time Andre Tippett is in the Hall of Fame."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.andre4hof.com/ |title=Tippett for HOF website |work=Andre4hof.com |access-date=November 28, 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080507162143/http://www.andre4hof.com/ |archive-date=May 7, 2008 }}</ref> He was selected to the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] for the class of 2008.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3227493 |title=Redskins' Green, Monk headline HOF class; Tagliabue shut out again |work=[[ESPN]] |publisher=Associated Press|date=February 2, 2008 |access-date=November 28, 2008}}</ref>

Tippett was inducted into the [[National Jewish Sports Hall of Fame]] in April 2009.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.boston.com/sports/football/patriots/reiss_pieces/2009/02/honor_for_andre.html|title=Honor for Andre Tippett – Reiss' Pieces|publisher=Boston Globe|date=February 12, 2009|access-date=February 12, 2009| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090215194013/http://boston.com/sports/football/patriots/reiss_pieces/2009/02/honor_for_andre.html| archive-date= February 15, 2009 }}</ref> In May 2012, he was inducted into the [[Alabama Sports Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.sjlmag.com/2012/05/patriots-great-andre-tippett-newest.html |title=Southern Jewish Life Magazine - covering the Jewish communities of Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, and NW Florida<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=April 23, 2018 |archive-date=April 23, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180423170032/http://www.sjlmag.com/2012/05/patriots-great-andre-tippett-newest.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

On November 13, 2021, Andre Tippett was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]].

==Personal life==
He is married to Rhonda Tippett (née Kenney) with three daughters, Janea Tippett, Asia Barnes, and Madison, and one son, [[Coby Tippett|Coby]]. A former Baptist, Tippett [[Conversion to Judaism|converted to Judaism]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rosenberg |first=Steven A. |date=December 13, 2014 |title=Patriots' Hall of Famer Andre Tippett lights the menorah |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/regionals/south/2014/12/14/patriots-hall-famer-andre-tippett-lights-menorah/22a1lPgYb1iHrC1NrTYBcO/story.html |access-date=2023-11-16 |website=BostonGlobe.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Parr |first=Molly |date=July 16, 2012 |title=Four Questions with Andre Tippett, Former Patriots Linebacker |url=http://www.jewishboston.com/read/four-questions-with-andre-tippett-former-patriots-linebacker/ |access-date=2023-11-16 |website=JewishBoston |language=en-US}}</ref> He currently lives in [[Sharon, Massachusetts]], and is a [[Pop Warner football]] coach.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.sharonpopwarner.net/rosters.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100829173401/http://www.sharonpopwarner.net/rosters.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 29, 2010 |title=Sharon Pop Warner Rosters |work=sharonpopwarner.com |access-date=January 30, 2012 }}</ref>

Tippett has also studied [[martial arts]] for over three decades.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.aeispeakers.com/speakerbio.php?SpeakerID=2283|title=Tippett Andre {{!}} Bio of Tippett Andre {{!}} AEI Speakers Bureau|website=www.aeispeakers.com|access-date=February 6, 2017}}</ref> He holds a seventh degree blackbelt in Uechi-ryu karate,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.stoughtondojo.com/staff/staff.html|title=Okinawan Karate Club - Staff|website=www.stoughtondojo.com|access-date=June 25, 2017}}</ref><ref name="g455">{{cite web | title=Second Act: Andre Tippett finds serenity in karate | website=NFL.com | date=2013-07-30 | url=https://www.nfl.com/news/second-act-andre-tippett-finds-serenity-in-karate-0ap1000000223815 | access-date=2024-09-13}}</ref> and is certified under the Okinawa Karate-do Association based in Okinawa, Japan.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.patriots.com/team/history/hall-of-fame/andre-tippett|title=Andre Tippett|date=March 9, 2015|newspaper=New England Patriots|access-date=February 6, 2017|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170207031743/http://www.patriots.com/team/history/hall-of-fame/andre-tippett|archive-date=February 7, 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref>

He currently serves as the executive director of Community Affairs for the New England Patriots.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.profootballhof.com/news/2005/01/news-andre-tippett-notes-and-quotes|title=Andre Tippett - Notes & Quotes | Pro Football Hall of Fame|website=pfhof}}</ref>

His son Coby played football for the [[University of Rhode Island]] as a kick returner and defensive back, He was invited to Rookie Mini Camp with the New England Patriots, and recently played for the [[Arlington Renegades]] and [[Houston Roughnecks (2020)|Houston Roughnecks]] of the [[XFL (2020)|XFL.]]

'''Andre Trevor Ware''' (born July 31, 1968) is an American [[sports analyst]] and [[sports commentator|commentator]], and a former professional [[gridiron football|football]] player. He played professionally as a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL) and [[NFL Europe]]. Ware played [[college football]] for the [[Houston Cougars football|Houston Cougars]], winning the [[Heisman Trophy]] and [[Davey O'Brien Award]] in 1989. He was the first black quarterback to receive the Heisman.<ref name="Undefeated">{{Cite web |url=https://andscape.com/features/nfl-analyst-andre-ware-first-black-quarterback-to-win-heisman/ |title=Andre Ware isn't just an analyst, he's the first black quarterback to win the Heisman |last=Bembry |first=Jerry |date=2017-11-23 |website=[[Andscape]] |language=en-US |access-date=2019-03-20}}</ref> In the [[1990 NFL draft]], Ware was selected in the first round by the [[Detroit Lions]] with the seventh overall pick. He was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2004.

==College career==

Ware grew up in the [[Galveston, Texas]] region, hoping to play football at the [[Texas Longhorns football|University of Texas]]. He said "I was going to Texas. All they had to do was lie to me and tell me I was going to play quarterback once I got there. Thank goodness they told me the truth [that] they were going to move me to defense".<ref name="cfl20140421">{{cite episode | series=College Football Live | credits=Weissman, Steve (host); Ware, Andre; Schad, Joe | network=ESPN | airdate=2014-04-21}}</ref> After graduating from [[Dickinson High School (Texas)|Dickinson High School]], Ware instead played at the [[Houston Cougars football|University of Houston]], where he won the [[Heisman Trophy]] in 1989, along with the [[Davey O'Brien Award]], the latter award given to the most outstanding college quarterback of the year.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1989 Heisman Trophy Voting |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/awards/heisman-1989.html |access-date=2024-10-11 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> That season - his junior year - averaging 52 passes per contest (365-of-578, 63.1%), he threw for 4,699 yards (427.18 yds/g or 127 yds/quarter), 46 touchdowns,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.heisman.com/heisman-winners/andre-ware/|title=Andre Ware}}</ref> and set 27 [[NCAA]] records over the span of 11 games, seven of which he sat during the fourth quarter. Many of the records (including the notable 340 yards/5 TDs in the first quarter and 517 yards/6 TDs thrown in one half, set on October 21, 1989, in a 95–21 rout against the [[SMU Mustangs]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nfl.com/news/ten-unbreakable-college-football-records-0ap2000000356173#:~:text=%EE%80%80Most%EE%80%81%20%EE%80%80passing%EE%80%81%20%EE%80%80yards%EE%80%81%2C%20%EE%80%80one%EE%80%81%20%EE%80%80half%EE%80%81%20%EE%80%80Record%EE%80%81%3A%20517%2C%20by,on%20the%20same%20field%20with%20a%20Houston%20|title = Ten unbreakable college football records|website = [[NFL.com]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.reviewjournal.com/sports/sports-columns/ron-kantowski/qb-andre-ware-led-the-revolution-at-houston/ |title=QB Andre Ware led the revolution at Houston |website=reviewjournal.com |date=September 19, 2014 |access-date=2023-04-01}}</ref>) were thanks to the innovative use of the [[run and shoot offense]], which his successor, [[David Klingler]], also used to great effect.  The [[1989 Houston Cougars football team|1989 Cougars]] were the first FBS team to have a 4,000-yard passer, [[Chuck Weatherspoon|1,000-yard rusher]], and [[Manny Hazard|1,000-yard receiver]] in the same season,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Khan Jr. |first=Sam |date=2014-08-07 |title=25 years later, Andre Ware's season matters |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/page/theseason0807ware/houston-andre-ware-changed-game-25-years-ago |access-date=2024-05-23 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref> where they ended the season 9–2 after averaging 624.9 y/g and ranked the #14 team in the nation by the [[Associated Press]], but were on probation, making Ware the only quarterback to win the Heisman while playing for a team on probation.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.heisman.com/heisman-winners/andre-ware/ | title=Andre Ware }}</ref> He then declared for the [[NFL draft]], forgoing his senior year.

==Professional football career==
Ware became the top draft pick of the [[Detroit Lions]] in the [[1990 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1990 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1990/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-24 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Head coach [[Wayne Fontes]] overrode the advice of the team's scouting director, who resigned the next day.  Ware joined the Lions for the [[1990 NFL season|1990 season]], teaming with the previous Heisman Trophy winner from 1988, [[Barry Sanders]]. Ware spent four years with Detroit, playing 14 games and starting six: Coach Fontes insisted on starting the oft-injured [[Rodney Peete]], and usually replacing Peete with [[Erik Kramer]] when Peete was hurt or played poorly. Fontes generally only played Ware when the Lions were out of the playoffs or already losing a game by a wide margin. Ware's best stretch came late in the [[1992 NFL season|1992 season]] when the Lions were out of the playoffs: he won two of three games.

In [[1994 NFL season|1994]] Ware was signed by the [[Minnesota Vikings]], but was released before the start of the season. He ended up on the roster of the [[Las Vegas Raiders|Los Angeles Raiders]], but was released after several games without being activated.  In 1995, he was signed by the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]], one of the NFL's two [[expansion team]]s that year.  As a former Heisman Trophy winner, Ware's presence created much local excitement in Jacksonville,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1356&dat=19950203&id=NBwVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=wQcEAAAAIBAJ&pg=4888,772642|title=Ocala Star-Banner - Google News Archive Search|website=news.google.com}}</ref> but ultimately Ware was cut from the team the week before the regular season began.

It is debated why Ware failed in the NFL despite a prolific college career. While some have argued that Ware's coaches never gave him a fair chance to develop, others have noticed that he was [[System quarterback|unable to adapt to an offensive system]] other than the run-and-shoot offense at Houston.<ref name = "Undefeated" />

Ware also played in the [[Canadian Football League]] with the [[Ottawa Rough Riders]], the [[BC Lions]] and the [[Toronto Argonauts]] (where he backed up fellow Heisman winner [[Doug Flutie]]).  He spent five games with the [[Berlin Thunder]], a German [[NFL Europe]] team.

==Broadcaster==
Since 2002, Ware has been a part of the [[Houston Texans]]' radio broadcast team with [[Marc Vandermeer]].

Since 2003, Ware has been a college football analyst for [[ESPN College Football|ESPN]]. From 2003 until 2008, he called games on [[ESPN College Football|ESPN]], ESPN2 and [[College Football on ABC|ESPN on ABC]]. In July 2009, ESPN announced that Ware would team up with long-time SEC broadcaster [[Dave Neal]] in the fall of 2009 as color commentator for [[ESPN Regional Television]]'s coverage of [[Southeastern Conference]] Football. Ware continued in this role until 2013. From 2014 through 2019, he called games for ESPN's [[SEC Network]], then joined the ESPN College Football Friday Primetime team in 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://espnmediazone.com/us/bios/ware_andre/|title=Andre Ware}}</ref>

'''Andre Le'Melle Weathers''' (born August 6, 1976) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player.  He played [[college football]] at the [[University of Michigan]] from 1995 to 1998 and was a member of the [[1997 Michigan Wolverines football team|1997 team]] that won the national championship.  He later played football for the [[New York Giants]] in 2000 and 2001, but his career was cut short by a knee injury.

==University of Michigan==
Weathers was a standout wide receiver and defensive back at [[Flint Central High School]], and earned a scholarship to play [[defensive back]] at the [[University of Michigan]]. Weathers was a defensive back for the Wolverines for four years from 1995 to 1998.<ref name=Stat>{{cite web|title=Michigan Football Statistic Archive Query Page |publisher=University of Michigan |url=http://stats.ath.umich.edu/football/footstart.php |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20040907204739/http://stats.ath.umich.edu/football/footstart.php |archivedate=2004-09-07 }}</ref>  He played on [[1997 Michigan Wolverines football team|Michigan's 1997 national championship team]] and had a 43-yard interception run-back for the winning touchdown in a 20–14 victory over Ohio State.<ref>{{cite news|author=Paul Daugherty|title=Of course, Buckeyes lose again|newspaper=The Cincinnati Enquirer|date=November 23, 1997 }}</ref>  Weathers also had a key sack of [[Ryan Leaf]] in Michigan's victory over Washington State in the [[1998 Rose Bowl]].  With the media attention focused on his teammate [[Charles Woodson]], Weathers was sometimes referred to by the press in 1997 as Michigan's "other cornerback."<ref>{{cite news|title=Michigan's 'Other Cornerback'|date=December 31, 1997|newspaper=Press-Telegram (Long Beach, CA)|url=http://nl.newsbank.com/nl-search/we/Archives?p_product=LB&p_theme=lb&p_action=search&p_maxdocs=200&p_topdoc=1&p_text_direct-0=0EAE91EE39731BDC&p_field_direct-0=document_id&p_perpage=10&p_sort=YMD_date:D&s_trackval=GooglePM}}</ref>  Because of Woodson's abilities, opponents regularly "threw at Weathers, not wanting to test Woodson."<ref name=OH/>  Weathers noted, "I like a challenge, but when you're expecting every ball to come at you, well, sometimes you want a little break."<ref name=OH>{{cite news|author=Rob Oller|title=HE DOESN'T TALK THE TALK BUT WOLVERINES CORNERBACK CAN WALK THE WALK|newspaper=Columbus Dispatch, Columbus, Ohio|date=November 18, 1998}}</ref>  In 1998, following Woodson's departure, Weathers was the leader of a Michigan secondary that remained one of the best in college football.<ref name=OH/><ref>{{cite news|author=Jim Cnockaert|title=Michigan secondary one of nation's best even without Woodson|newspaper=The Grand Rapids Press, Grand Rapids, Mich.|date=August 23, 1998|page=E.1}}</ref>

During his four-year career at Michigan, Weathers had 84 tackles and 5 interceptions.<ref name=Stat/>

==New York Giants==
In April 1999, Weathers was selected by the [[New York Giants]] in the sixth round of the [[1999 NFL draft]] with the 205th overall pick.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1999 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1999/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>  He signed with the Giants in July 1999.<ref>{{cite news|title=Transactions|newspaper=The New York Times|date=July 30, 1999}}</ref>  During the Giants' 1999 training camp, Weathers was nicknamed "Nonchalant" for his somewhat carefree attitude.<ref name=Bergen/>  Weathers made the final cut and played in the Giants' season opener against the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]].<ref name=Bergen>{{cite news|author=Vinny DiTrani|title=GIANTS WEATHERS WILL JOIN THE PARTY|newspaper=The Record, Bergen County, N.J.|date=October 28, 2000|page=S.02}}</ref>  In that game, his first in the NFL, Weathers intercepted a pass off [[Trent Dilfer]] and returned it for the winning touchdown as the Giants defeated Buccaneers, 17–13.<ref name=NYT>{{cite news|author=Frank Litsky|title=PRO FOOTBALL; Giants' Weathers A Quick Study|newspaper=The New York Times|date=September 15, 1999|url=https://select.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=F60D13FD3D580C768DDDA00894D1494D81}}</ref>

After the Tampa Bay game, Weathers was the subject of a feature stories in ''[[The New York Times]]'' and the ''[[New York Daily News]]''.<ref name=NYT/><ref name=NYDN/>  Weathers described his thoughts as he intercepted Dilfer's pass, "I know he couldn't see me, because I couldn't even see him. I didn't actually see the ball until it was right on top of me.  My eyes got big, and I didn't have time to think about it. I thought only about holding onto the ball and going in. The end zone was there, and when I didn't see anybody in front of me I knew it was a touchdown."<ref name=NYT/><ref name=NYDN/>  The ''Daily News'' reported, "Only a week ago, rookie Andre Weathers was sweating out the final cuts, and if not for the injuries to [[Jason Sehorn]] and [[Conrad Hamilton]] that created a need for cornerbacks, who knows?  But there he was yesterday, making perhaps the biggest play of the 17-13 win over the Bucs as he returned an interception eight yards for the go-ahead touchdown in the third quarter."<ref name=NYDN>{{cite news|author=John Harper|title=ROOKIE'S BIG SCORE WEATHERS THE STORM|newspaper=[[New York Daily News]]|date=September 13, 1999|page=59}}</ref>  Veteran cornerback [[Phillippi Sparks]] said of Weathers, "That kid can be special if he works at it.  He reminds me of myself. He's a little lackadaisical in practice because he knows he has skills. If he works at it, he can be a great player, and I won't let him do anything else."<ref name=NYT/>

Weathers appeared in nine games for the Giants during the [[1999 NFL season]].  However, he tore the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee during a November 1999 game against the [[Indianapolis Colts]].<ref>{{cite news|author=Bill Pennington|title=PRO FOOTBALL: EXTRA POINTS; Ruling Leaves Giants Empty|newspaper=The New York Times|date=November 15, 1999|url=https://select.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=F30810FD39590C768DDDA80994D1494D81}}</ref>  Weathers underwent knee surgery in November 1999.<ref>{{cite news|author=John Harper|newspaper=New York Daily news|title=WEATHERS MAY RETURN VS. FALCONS|date=October 6, 2000|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/sports/2000/10/06/2000-10-06_weathers_may_return_vs__falc.html}}</ref>

Weathers returned to the Giants at the end of October 2000.<ref>{{cite news|author=Paul Schwartz|title=WEATHERS CAN'T WAIT ANY LONGER|newspaper=New York Post|date=October 28, 2000|url=https://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/nypost/access/68883876.html?dids=68883876:68883876&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Oct+28,+2000&author=PAUL+SCHWARTZ&pub=New+York+Post&desc=WEATHERS+CAN%27T+WAIT+ANY+LONGER&pqatl=google|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130201051548/http://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/nypost/access/68883876.html?dids=68883876:68883876&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Oct+28,+2000&author=PAUL+SCHWARTZ&pub=New+York+Post&desc=WEATHERS+CAN'T+WAIT+ANY+LONGER&pqatl=google|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 1, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Stephen Edelson|title=Weathers' return bolsters Giants' secondary|publisher=Gannett News Service|date=October 28, 2000}}</ref>  At the time of his return, Weathers noted, "It's going to be exciting and nervous at the same time. I'm anxious to get out there and see what I can do."<ref name=NYDN/>  The ''New York Daily News'' reported, "Weathers doesn't pretend that the knee is as sound as it had been. Most doctors agree that it takes about two years after major knee surgery for a 100% recovery."<ref name=NYDNGola>{{cite news|author=Hank Gola|title=GIANTS HOPE SUB WEATHERS RETURN|newspaper=[[New York Daily News]]|date=October 28, 2000|page=70}}</ref>  In his first game back, he immediately sustained a tear in the anterior cruciate knee ligaments to end his season.  At the time, the ''New York Post'' noted: "This is especially cruel news for Weathers, who last Sunday made his debut this season. A rookie in 1999, Weathers showed plenty of promise before tearing his left ACL in the ninth game of the season. The Giants were cautious in bringing Weathers back, but he reinjured the same knee in the 24–7 victory over the Philadelphia Eagles, will again need surgery and faces another year-long rehab."<ref>{{cite news|author=Paul Schwartz|title=INJURY BUG TAKES BITE OUT OF FASSEL'S BENCH|newspaper=New York Post|date=November 3, 2000|url=https://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/nypost/access/68884470.html?dids=68884470:68884470&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Nov+03,+2000&author=PAUL+SCHWARTZ&pub=New+York+Post&desc=INJURY+BUG+TAKES+BITE+OUT+OF+FASSEL%27S+BENCH&pqatl=google|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130131170135/http://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/nypost/access/68884470.html?dids=68884470:68884470&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Nov+03,+2000&author=PAUL+SCHWARTZ&pub=New+York+Post&desc=INJURY+BUG+TAKES+BITE+OUT+OF+FASSEL'S+BENCH&pqatl=google|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 31, 2013}}</ref>  Weathers attempted a comeback with the Giants in 2001, but did not make the team.<ref>{{cite news|author=Paul Schwartz|title=GIANTS DEFENSE NOT SURE WHAT WEATHERS WILL BE|newspaper=New York Post|date=August 11, 2000|url=https://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/nypost/access/68872814.html?dids=68872814:68872814&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Aug+11,+2000&author=PAUL+SCHWARTZ&pub=New+York+Post&desc=GIANTS+DEFENSE+NOT+SURE+WHAT+WEATHERS+WILL+BE&pqatl=google|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121104013830/http://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/nypost/access/68872814.html?dids=68872814:68872814&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Aug+11,+2000&author=PAUL+SCHWARTZ&pub=New+York+Post&desc=GIANTS+DEFENSE+NOT+SURE+WHAT+WEATHERS+WILL+BE&pqatl=google|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 4, 2012}}</ref>  He was released by the Giants in August 2001.<ref>{{cite news|title=2001 Professional Football|newspaper=Houston Chronicle|date=August 26, 2001}}</ref>

==Later life==
After retiring from football, Weathers returned to his hometown, [[Flint, Michigan]].  He worked as a high school football coach at [[Flint Central High School]] and with the Genesee County Patriots semi-pro team.<ref>{{cite news|author=Bryn Mickle|title=Looking for Super Bowl super fans? Flint-area has them|newspaper=The Flint Journal|date=February 2, 2008|url=http://www.mlive.com/news/index.ssf/2008/02/looking_for_super_bowl_super_f.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Dan Nilsen|title=Closing of Flint Central ends decades of football tradition|newspaper=The Flint Journal|date=August 27, 2009|url=http://highschoolsports.mlive.com/news/article/-1218990768132034871/closing-of-flint-central-ends-decades-of-football-tradition/}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Jeff Meade|title=Well-prepared Timberwolves travel to Flint for season-opener Saturday|newspaper=The Monroe Evening News, Monroe, Michigan|date=July 6, 2007|url=http://nl.newsbank.com/nl-search/we/Archives?p_product=MONP&p_multi=MEVB&p_theme=monp&p_action=search&p_maxdocs=200&p_topdoc=1&p_text_direct-0=11A495D5134D0658&p_field_direct-0=document_id&p_perpage=10&p_sort=YMD_date:D&s_trackval=GooglePM}}</ref>

'''Andrew Greene''' (born September 24, 1969) is a former professional [[gridiron football]] [[offensive tackle]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) and [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL). Greene, a nine-year CFL veteran, spent much of his career with the [[Saskatchewan Roughriders]]. The four-time CFL all-star was named the league's top offensive lineman in 2003.

==Early life==
At [[Pickering High School, Ajax|Pickering High School]] in [[Ajax, Ontario|Ajax]], [[Ontario]], Greene lettered in football, basketball, rugby, and track & field.

==College career==
At [[Indiana University Bloomington]], Greene was a four-year letterman and a three-year starter. He was named twice named "Indiana's Outstanding Offensive Lineman", and as a senior, also won first-team All-Big Ten Conference honors and was a second-team All-American.

==Professional career==
Greene joined the Roughriders in 1997 after spending time with the [[Miami Dolphins]], [[Seattle Seahawks]] and [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] of the NFL. He has appeared in 116 regular season games, nine playoff games and one Grey Cup. On February 21, 2007, Greene signed as a free agent with the [[Winnipeg Blue Bombers]], starting all 18 games for them. He went on to play for the Bombers in the [[95th Grey Cup]] in [[Toronto]], only to lose to his former team, the Roughriders. On September 17, 2008, Greene signed with the Toronto Argonauts and was assigned to their practice roster. At the time of his signing, he became the oldest active player in the CFL.

On January 26, 2009, Greene was released by the Argonauts.

On May 25, 2009, the Saskatchewan Roughriders signed Greene after which he promptly announced his retirement showing his desire to retire as a Roughrider. Saskatchewan Roughrider Club President/CEO Jim Hopson stated, "When a player such as Andrew wants to end a long successful career in Green and White, we gladly do our part to help. It's our way of showing appreciation for all the years of dedication and hard work he put into this organization."

'''Andre Maurice Woolfolk''' (born January 26, 1980) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Tennessee Titans]]. He was selected by the Titans in the first round of the [[2003 NFL draft]] after playing [[college football]] at [[Oklahoma Sooners football|Oklahoma]]. Woolfolk was also an offseason member of the [[New York Jets]].

==Early life==
A native of [[Denver]], he attended [[Thomas Jefferson High School (Denver)|Thomas Jefferson High School]], where he played for the [[high school football|football]] team and was teammates with [[Daniel Graham]]<ref name="titans"/> Woolfolk recorded 171 tackles and 19 interceptions in high school.<ref name="titans"/>

==College career==
Woolfolk played [[college football]] for the [[Oklahoma Sooners football|Oklahoma]] from 1998 to 2002.<ref name="sr">{{cite web | url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/andre-woolfolk-1.html | title=Andre Woolfolk | publisher=sports-reference.com | accessdate=June 5, 2024}}</ref> He redshirted in 1998.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.crimsonandcreammachine.com/2018/8/15/17693102/2018-oklahoma-sooners-countdown-to-kickoff-17-days-andre-woolfolk-receiver-cornerback-nebraska-2000 | title=2018 Oklahoma Sooners Countdown to Kickoff | publisher=crimsonandcreammachine.com | date=August 15, 2018 | accessdate=June 5, 2024 | author=Oliveras, Seth}}</ref> He played both [[wide receiver]] and defensive back for the Sooners.<ref name="sr"/> As a receiver, Woolfolk caught 11 passes for 129 yards and one touchdown in 1999, 39 passes for 573 yards and five touchdowns in 2000, and six passes for 134 yards in 2001.<ref name="sr"/> Woolfolk switched to defensive back full-time after the fifth game of the 2001 season.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.oudaily.com/sports/ou-football-andre-woolfolk-gives-trejan-bridges-advice-about-moving-to-defense-says-trust-the/article_dfcf29f0-def3-11e9-8cf5-d33860617761.html | title=OU football: Andre Woolfolk gives Trejan Bridges advice about moving to defense, says 'trust the process' | publisher=oudaily.com | date=September 24, 2019 | accessdate=June 5, 2024 | author=Stoia, George}}</ref> He earned third-team All-[[Big 12 Conference|Big 12]] honors in 2000 and 2001 and was also a member of the Oklahoma team that won the national championship in 2000.<ref name="titans"/>

==Professional career==
===Tennessee Titans===
Woolfolk was selected by the [[Tennessee Titans]] in the first round, with the 28th overall pick, of the [[2003 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2003 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2003/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He officially signed with the team on July 25, 2003. He played in six games, starting two, for the Titans during his rookie year in 2003, recording 18 solo tackles, five assisted tackles, one interception and five pass breakups. He was placed on injured reserve on December 23, 2003. Woolfolk appeared in 10 games, starting two, in 2004, totaling 42 solo tackles, seven assisted tackles, one interception and six pass breakups. He was placed on injured reserve for the second consecutive year on December 31, 2004. He played in 13 games, starting seven, for the Titans during the 2005 season, accumulating 42 solo tackles, 13 assisted tackles, one interception, seven pass breakups, one forced fumble and one fumble recovery. Woolfolk appeared in 10 games, starting one, in 2006, recording six solo tackles and three assisted tackles.<ref name="pfr">{{Cite web |title=Andre Woolfolk Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WoolAn20.htm |access-date=2025-07-04 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

He was placed on injured reserve for the third time on August 14, 2007, and was released by the Titans on August 23, 2007.<ref name="pfr" /> Overall, he played in 39 games, starting 12, during his NFL career, totaling 108 solo tackles, 28 assisted tackles, three interceptions, 18 pass breakups, one forced fumble and one fumble recovery.<ref name="pfr" /> All three of his interceptions were thrown by [[David Carr (American football)|David Carr]].<ref name="nyt"/>

===New York Jets===
Woolfolk signed with the [[New York Jets]] on March 4, 2008, but was released on July 30, 2008.<ref name="pfr" />

In 2021, ''[[The New York Times]]'' named Woolfolk the biggest [[draft bust]] ever chosen with the 28th overall pick.<ref name="nyt">{{cite web | url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/2527738/2021/04/23/the-ultimate-nfl-draft-bust-round-from-ryan-leaf-to-johnny-manziel-the-worst-picks-ever-at-each-slot/ | title=The ultimate NFL Draft bust round: From Ryan Leaf to Johnny Manziel, the worst picks ever at each slot | publisher=[[The New York Times]] | date=April 23, 2021 | accessdate=June 5, 2024 | author=Howe, Jeff}}</ref>

==Personal life==
He is a cousin of [[Butch Woolfolk]].<ref name="titans"/>

Waters was regarded as one of the NFL's most aggressive players, serving as an integral part of one of the league's top defenses. On November 20, 2006, Waters died by suicide and was subsequently diagnosed with [[chronic traumatic encephalopathy]] (CTE). He is one of at least 345 [[List of NFL players with chronic traumatic encephalopathy|NFL players to be diagnosed after death with CTE]], which is caused by repeated hits to the head.{{cite news |title=The driving force behind Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE) |website=Concussion Legacy Foundation |url=https://concussionfoundation.org/cte-resources/subconcussive-impacts |access-date=July 2, 2023 |archive-date=July 2, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230702123543/https://concussionfoundation.org/cte-resources/subconcussive-impacts |url-status=dead }}{{cite news |author=Ken Belson and Benjamin Mueller |url= https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/20/sports/football/cte-study-concussions-brain-tackle.html |title=Collective Force of Head Hits, Not Just the Number of Them, Increases Odds of C.T.E. The largest study of chronic traumatic encephalopathy to date found that the cumulative force of head hits absorbed by players in their careers is the best predictor of future brain disease. |work= [[The New York Times]] |date=June 20, 2023 |access-date=July 2, 2023 }} ==Early life== Waters was born in [[Belle Glade, Florida]] and grew up in [[extreme poverty]] in rural Florida, and attended [[Pahokee High School]]. Waters received some attention in high school but ended up attending [[Cheyney Wolves|Cheyney University]]{{cite web |last=Habib|first=Hal| url=https://www.palmbeachpost.com/sports/football-killed-him-the-legacy-pahokee-andre-waters/V7LRMnWBQeFslWPw06z9WL/ | title='Football killed him': The legacy of Pahokee's Andre Waters|date=September 14, 2010|work=Palm Beach Post|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20121011095902/http://www.palmbeachpost.com/news/sports/football-killed-him-the-legacy-of-pahokees-andre-w/nL9wz/|archivedate=October 11, 2012 | accessdate=March 18, 2013}} At [[Cheyney University of Pennsylvania]] Waters was recognized as [[Pennsylvania State Athletic Conference|All-PSAC]] three straight years.{{cite web | url=http://www.cheyney.edu/athletics/news/15629/5856/no.aspx | title=Esteem Alum Andre Waters Passes Away | accessdate=May 6, 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180507085133/http://www.cheyney.edu/athletics/news/15629/5856/no.aspx | archive-date=May 7, 2018 | url-status=dead }} ==Professional career == In [[1984 NFL season|1984]], Waters was signed as an [[undrafted free agent]] by [[Philadelphia Eagles]] head coach [[Marion Campbell]]. He returned a [[Kickoff (American football)|kickoff]] for an 89-yard game-winning [[touchdown]] against the [[Washington Redskins]] as a rookie in 1984. When [[Buddy Ryan]] took over for Campbell in [[1986 NFL season|1986]], he welcomed Waters' aggressive style as a fierce tackler and ferocious hitter, earning Waters a position in the starting lineup for the next eight years. He blossomed under defensive coordinator [[Bud Carson]]. His tackle of [[Los Angeles Rams]] [[quarterback]] [[Jim Everett]] in [[1988 NFL season|1988]] led to a rule prohibiting defensive players from hitting quarterbacks below the waist while they are still in the pocket; for a while, it was unofficially termed the "Andre Waters Rule". NFL broadcaster [[Dan Dierdorf]] notoriously nicknamed the Eagles defender "Dirty Waters". He scored a touchdown in 1989 when he took a [[lateral pass|lateral]] from [[William Frizzell]] after [[Reggie White]] caused a fumble by [[New York Giants]] quarterback [[Phil Simms]]. Waters served as part of the Eagles' defensive unit that was regarded as one of the league's all-time best, in [[1991 Philadelphia Eagles season|1991]] ranking first statistically in both run and pass defense, as well as total defense. His hard-hitting style translated into leading the team in tackles for four seasons and endeared him with Philadelphia fans but often led to penalties and fines for some of his tackles. He led the Eagles in tackles in 1986, [[1987 NFL season|1987]], 1988 and 1991. He recorded 15 [[interception]]s in 156 games. In 1994, he was replaced by [[Mike Zordich]] due to his contract ending. Waters finished his career playing for Ryan with the [[Arizona Cardinals]] for two seasons. == Coaching career == After retiring as a player, Waters worked as a college football coach. In 1996, he joined the staff of [[Stump Mitchell]] at [[Morgan State Bears football|Morgan State]] as defensive backs coach.{{cite web|last=Kubatko|first=Roch Eric|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1996/03/28/morgan-hires-ex-eagle-waters/|title=Morgan hires ex-Eagle Waters|work=The Baltimore Sun|date=March 28, 1996|access-date=May 6, 2018}} The following year under head coach [[Jim Leavitt]], Waters took the same position on the upstart [[South Florida Bulls football|South Florida]] football program.{{cite web|url=https://www.tampabay.com/sports/college/revisiting-the-inaugural-1997-usf-bulls-football-roster/2334221/|title=Revisiting the inaugural 1997 USF Bulls football roster|work=Tampa Bay Times|date=August 18, 2017|last=Knight|first=Joey|access-date=May 6, 2018}} He remained in that position until 1999.{{cite web|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070111192348/http://www.sptimes.com/2006/12/11/Sports/The_mysterious_death_.shtml|archivedate=January 11, 2007|title=The mysterious death of Andre Waters|last=Scheiber|first=Dave|work=St. Petersburg Times|date=December 11, 2006|url=http://www.sptimes.com/2006/12/11/Sports/The_mysterious_death_.shtml|accessdate=May 6, 2018}} In 2000, Waters left South Florida to join the [[St. Louis Rams]] of the NFL as a coaching intern for training camp under Defensive Coordinator, Bud Carson. Leavitt made Waters choose between South Florida and the internship out of concern that Waters would miss too much preparation time with South Florida. After his Rams internship, Waters returned to Tampa to be defensive coordinator at [[Paul R. Wharton High School]] in 2000. In 2001, Waters moved back to the college level as defensive backs coach at [[Alabama State Hornets football|Alabama State]].{{citation|title=Coach Andre Waters|url=https://archive.org/stream/saintaugustinesc37534unse#page/20/mode/2up/search/Andre+Waters|work=Saint Augustine's College vs. North Carolina Central University|publisher=Saint Augustine's College|place=Raleigh, NC|year=2002|page=20}}{{cite web|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20040821150421/http://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/news/whereAreTheyNowDetail.jsp?id=13323|archivedate=August 21, 2004|title= Where Are They Now: SS Andre Waters|url=http://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/news/whereAreTheyNowDetail.jsp?id=13323|last=Kravitz|first=Gary|publisher=Philadelphia Eagles|date=August 4, 2004|accessdate=May 6, 2018}} In 2002, Waters joined the [[Detroit Lions]] in his second stint as an NFL coaching intern.{{cite web|url=https://www.nfl.info/nflmedia/News/2002News/MinorityCoachingFellowship2002.htm|title=Minority coaching fellowship attracts record 83 participants; coordinators Lewis & Lynn grads of program|publisher=NFL|date=August 26, 2002|accessdate=May 6, 2018}} He later coached at [[St. Augustine's College (Raleigh)|St. Augustine's]] from 2002 to 2005 as defensive coordinator upon the football program's return from a 35-year hiatus.{{cite web|url=https://onnidan.com/01-02/news/mar/best0328.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020822030218/http://www.onnidan.com/01-02/news/mar/best0328.htm|url-status=usurped|archive-date=August 22, 2002|title= Football is officially back at St. Aug's and Shaw|last=Best|first=Bonitta|work=Triangle Tribune|date=March 28, 2002|accessdate=May 6, 2018}} In 2006, Waters was defensive coordinator at [[Fort Valley State University#Athletics|Fort Valley State]].{{cite web|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070228194841/http://www.macon.com/mld/macon/16059523.htm|archivedate=February 28, 2007|title=FVSU assistant coach, ex-NFL player Andre Waters, dies|url=http://www.macon.com/mld/macon/16059523.htm|last=McPhail|first=Ayanna|work=Macon Telegraph|date=November 20, 2006|accessdate=May 6, 2018}} Waters described his disappointment in not getting a full-time NFL coaching job to ''[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]'' reporter Phil Sheridan.{{cite web|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20061129095147/http://www.philly.com/mld/philly/news/16062892.htm|archivedate=November 29, 2006|title=Suicide of ex-Eagle Andre Waters hits hard|url=http://www.philly.com:80/mld/philly/news/16062892.htm|last=Sheridan|first=Phil|work=Philadelphia Inquirer|date=November 21, 2006|accessdate=May 6, 2018|url-status=dead}} He remained very close to his former Eagles coach [[Buddy Ryan]], whom Waters said he tried to emulate in his own coaching career. ==Death== Waters died by suicide shortly after 1 a.m. on November 20, 2006, according to the [[Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office (Florida)|Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office]], dying of a gunshot to the head. He was at his home in [[Tampa, Florida]] where he was discovered by his girlfriend.{{cite news|first=Thomasi|last=McDonald |title=Former NFL player, St. Aug's coach dies |url=http://www.newsobserver.com/102/story/512849.html |work=News & Observer |date=2006-11-20 |accessdate=2006-11-20 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080922222249/http://www.newsobserver.com/102/story/512849.html |archivedate=September 22, 2008 }} He was buried at Foreverglades Cemetery in [[Belle Glade, Florida]]. Shortly after Waters' death, former [[Harvard University|Harvard]] defensive tackle and [[World Wrestling Entertainment|WWE]] wrestler [[Christopher Nowinski|Dr. Christopher Nowinski]], whose wrestling career was ended by [[post-concussion syndrome]] and has since written a book about the dangers of [[concussion]]s in contact sports, approached Waters' family and asked permission to have his brain tissue examined. After receiving permission, Nowinski had samples of Waters' brain tissue sent to neuropathologist Dr. [[Bennet Omalu]] at the [[University of Pittsburgh]]. Omalu believed, having examined the tissue, that Waters sustained brain damage from playing football: he went on to state that this led to Waters' [[Major depressive disorder|depression]].{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/01/18/sports/football/18waters.html|title=Expert Ties Ex-Player's Suicide to Brain Damage|last=Schwarz|first=Alan|work=The New York Times|date=January 18, 2007|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20081211080811/http://www.nytimes.com/2007/01/18/sports/football/18waters.html|archivedate=December 11, 2008|accessdate=May 5, 2018}} Omalu determined that Waters' brain tissue had developed [[chronic traumatic encephalopathy]] (CTE) and degenerated into that of an 80-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease, caused or hastened by the numerous concussions Waters sustained playing football.{{citation|title=Chronic traumatic encephalopathy in the National Football League|last=Cantu|first=Robert C.|journal=Neurosurgery|volume=61|issue=2|date=August 2007|pages=223–225|doi=10.1227/01.NEU.0000255514.73967.90|pmid = 17762733}} Waters was portrayed by actor [[Richard T. Jones]] in the 2015 film ''[[Concussion (2015 film)|Concussion]]''. ==See also== * [[List of NFL players with chronic traumatic encephalopathy]] ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Eagles75}} {{authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Waters, Andre}} [[Category:1962 births]] [[Category:2006 deaths]] [[Category:Players of American football with chronic traumatic encephalopathy]] [[Category:American football safeties]] [[Category:Alabama State Hornets football coaches]] [[Category:Arizona Cardinals players]] [[Category:Cheyney Wolves football players]] [[Category:Fort Valley State Wildcats football coaches]] [[Category:Morgan State Bears football coaches]] [[Category:Philadelphia Eagles players]] [[Category:St. Augustine's Falcons football coaches]] [[Category:South Florida Bulls football coaches]] [[Category:High school football coaches in Florida]] [[Category:Players of American football from Pahokee, Florida]] [[Category:Suicides by firearm in Florida]] [[Category:2006 suicides]] [[Category:Pahokee High School alumni]] [[Category:20th-century American sportsmen]]

He was selected in the first round of the [[1998 NFL draft]] by the [[Arizona Cardinals]]. ==Early life== Wadsworth was born in [[St. Croix, U.S. Virgin Islands]]. He attended Class A [[Florida Christian School]] in [[Miami-Dade County, Florida]], where he starred at [[tight end]] for the Florida Christian Patriots [[high school football]] team. Wadsworth was named first-team All-Dade County and voted all-conference and second-team all-state as a defensive lineman. Wadsworth decided to attend Florida State University, and played for the [[Florida State Seminoles football]] team as a [[Walk-on (sport term)|walk-on]] and eventually earned an [[athletic scholarship]]. He received second-team [[List of All-Atlantic Coast Conference football teams|All-Atlantic Coast Conference]] (ACC) honors his freshman, sophomore and junior seasons (1994–1996) as a [[defensive tackle]]. Despite being a potential top-10 NFL Draft pick after his junior season, he stayed for his senior year, citing a pinched nerve in his neck that forced him out of four games in 1996 as a concern regarding his physical capabilities to perform for [[Scout (sport)|scouts]] at full capacity. He switched from defensive tackle to left defensive end for his senior season, registering 59 tackles, 19 [[Tackle (football move)|tackles]] for a loss and 16 [[quarterback sack]]s, placing him second in both categories in the school's all-time records. One of four finalists for the [[Lombardi Award]], he was named first-team All-ACC and a consensus first-team [[1997 College Football All-America Team|All-American]]. He was also selected ACC Player of the Year, and ACC Defensive Player of the year in 1997. ==Professional career== ===1998 NFL draft=== Wadsworth bench pressed 500 pounds and had a personal best in the squat of 690.[https://web.archive.org/web/20000824105555/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/features/1998/weekly/980420/skysthelimit.html Sports Illustrated.com] The Steelers' college personnel director, Tom Modrak, said: "He's like a missile when he comes off the ball. He can keep his pads low and still run full speed. He's flexible, and he's around 280 pounds." Wadsworth was regarded as the No. 1 defensive prospect in the [[1998 NFL draft]].{{cite news|title=NFL Draft: War Room Value Board {{ndash}} Andre Wadsworth| url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/nfl/events/1998/nfldraft/topplayers/1.html | work=CNN|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060429150146/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/nfl/events/1998/nfldraft/topplayers/1.html|archive-date=April 29, 2006}}{{Cite web |last=Maisel |first=Ivan |author-link=Ivan Maisel |date=April 15, 1998 |title=The Sky's the Limit |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/features/1998/weekly/980420/skysthelimit.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000824105555/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/features/1998/weekly/980420/skysthelimit.html |archive-date=2000-08-24 |access-date=2025-08-25 |website=CNN/SI}} He was selected in the first round with the third overall pick by the [[Arizona Cardinals]], after [[Peyton Manning]] and [[Ryan Leaf]].{{Cite web |title=1998 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1998/draft.htm |access-date=March 29, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} {{NFL predraft | height ft = 6 | height in = 3 5/8 | weight = 278 | dash = 4.65 | ten split = | twenty split = | shuttle = 4.38 | cone drill = 7.42 | vertical = 35.5 | broad ft = 9 | broad in = 11 | bench = | wonderlic = | arm span = 34 1/4 | hand span = 10 1/4 | note = All values from [[NFL Combine]]{{Cite web |url=https://nflcombineresults.com/playerpage.php?i=22808 |title=Andre Wadsworth, Combine Results, DE - Florida State |website=nflcombineresults.com |access-date=October 8, 2022}}{{Cite web |url=https://ras.football/2019/12/20/andre-wadsworth-ras/ |title=Andre Wadsworth RAS |website=ras.football |access-date=October 8, 2022}} }} ===Arizona Cardinals=== A lengthy holdout ensued, centered almost directly on both his demand to be paid closer to the contracts signed by the two previous picks, [[Indianapolis Colts]]' [[Peyton Manning]] out of [[University of Tennessee]] at No. 1 and the [[San Diego Chargers]]' [[Ryan Leaf]] from [[Washington State University]] at No. 2 rather than one closer to [[Heisman Trophy]] winner [[Charles Woodson]] selected by the [[Oakland Raiders]] at No. 4, and a provision allowing him to void the contract before expiration if he chose to do so. The holdout lasted until the night before the season-opener (44 days) with a six-year, $42 million contract including a $10.49 million signing bonus (Manning received $11.6 million on a $48 million contract, Leaf got $11.2 million on a five-year contract totaling $31.2 million), though the player-triggered option out was never consummated.[https://web.archive.org/web/20110516152054/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-68455850.html Highbeam.com] He played in all 16 games his rookie season, finishing with 5.0 sacks and 57 tackles, including 42 solo. Bothered by a knee injury in 1999, he still managed to play in 11 games, tallying 2.0 sacks, 26 tackles, and his only career [[interception]]. Off-season knee surgery, the second of his career, held him out from most of the off-season activities, but still managed 13 tackles and one sack in nine games. At the conclusion of the [[2000 NFL season|2000 season]], Wadsworth underwent [[microfracture surgery]] on his right knee, the third surgery on that knee in his career, and [[arthroscopic surgery]] on the left on January 3 with non-team physician Richard Steadman. Possibly due to concerns after teammate [[Eric Swann]]'s semi-recovery from nine knee surgeries, the Arizona Cardinals released Wadsworth before offering a one-year, $512,000 tender that was eventually pulled off the table within days after it went unsigned. On January 28, 2007, the ''[[St. Petersburg Times]]'' reported that the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] were planning to give Wadsworth, now 32, a workout.[http://www.sptimes.com/2007/01/28/Bucs/Bucs_scrutinize_prosp.shtml St. Petersburg Times] The [[New York Jets]] gave Wadsworth a workout later in the offseason.{{cite news | last = Cimini | first = Rich | url = http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/football/jets/2007/03/27/2007-03-27_gang_takes_flier_on_wadsworth.html | title = Gang takes flier on Wadsworth | newspaper = [[New York Daily News]] | date = March 27, 2007 | access-date = March 30, 2007| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20070331082059/http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/football/jets/2007/03/27/2007-03-27_gang_takes_flier_on_wadsworth.html| archive-date= March 31, 2007 | url-status= live}} On March 26, 2007, the New York Jets signed Wadsworth to a minimum-based salary contract.[http://www.jetsinsider.net/ji/news.php?storyid=2033 New York Post] {{webarchive |url=https://archive.today/20070503092220/http://www.jetsinsider.net/ji/news.php?storyid=2033 |date=May 3, 2007 }} Wadsworth was also said to be healthy enough to compete for an outside linebacker position. He was selected by the [[New York Giants]] in the sixth round of the [[2008 NFL draft]]. Woodson played collegiately at the [[Kentucky Wildcats football|University of Kentucky]]. ==Early life== Born on [[Military base|post]] in [[Fort Lewis (Washington)|Fort Lewis, Washington]] where his mother, Robin Woodson, was stationed in the Army with his father (Andre W.) Woodson grew up a [[military brat (U.S. subculture)|military brat]], moving from post to post with his mother after his parents divorced when he was the age of two. He was raised by his mother as she continued her [[United States Army|Army]] service, eventually arriving in Radcliff, Kentucky, in 1994. He attended local schools nearby, Radcliff Middle School and [[North Hardin High School]], both in Radcliff, Kentucky (Hardin County Kentucky, located near [[Fort Knox|Fort Knox, Kentucky]]), where he lettered in basketball and football, which eventually led to his being noticed for his football potential by the [[University of Kentucky]]. ==College career== In 2003, Woodson was [[Recruiting (college athletics)|recruited]] to [[Kentucky Wildcats|Kentucky]]. During his freshman season, Woodson served as a backup to [[Shane Boyd]], and appeared in seven games (including one [[Starting lineup|start]]). For the 2005 season, Woodson was named as the starting quarterback. The Wildcats ended 2005 with a 3–8 record, with Woodson completing nearly 58 percent of his passes, while throwing for 1,644 yards. After the 2006 spring practice, it appeared Woodson would lose his position to his backup, [[Curtis Pulley]].{{cite news |last = Jonathan| first = Smith|title = Woodson, Pulley make giant strides over summer|pages = 1|publisher = The Kentucky Kernel| date = 2006-09-01| url = http://www.kykernel.com/home/index.cfm?event=displayArticle&ustory_id=bcdfb465-de5d-4f26-8751-f6d630f34968| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070927234724/http://www.kykernel.com/home/index.cfm?event=displayArticle&ustory_id=bcdfb465-de5d-4f26-8751-f6d630f34968| url-status = dead| archive-date = 2007-09-27| accessdate = 2007-04-03 }} Spurred by this, Woodson started spending more time lifting weights, began leading the team in practice, and soon became the choice for starting quarterback. The [[2006 Kentucky Wildcats football team|2006 season]], Woodson's junior season, was a breakout season, with Woodson leading the Wildcats to a 7–5 regular season, and their first [[Bowl game|bowl]] win in 22 years, in the [[Music City Bowl]]. He led both his team and the SEC in passing yards with 3,515,{{Citation|title=Kentucky Wildcat 2006 cumulative season statistics |year=2006 |url=http://www.ukathletics.com/stats/2006_07/football/teamcume.htm |accessdate=2007-04-03 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930201906/http://www.ukathletics.com/stats/2006_07/football/teamcume.htm |archivedate=2007-09-30 }} and became only the second Kentucky quarterback to throw 30 or more touchdowns in a single season.{{cite news | last = Low| first = Chris| title = Key playmakers in Cats' explosive attack returning| pages = 1| publisher = ESPN| date = 2007-03-29| url = https://www.espn.com/college-football/news/story?id=2816885| access-date = 2007-04-03}} On September 22, 2007, Woodson broke [[Trent Dilfer]]'s all-time NCAA record of 271 consecutive pass attempts without an interception against the [[Arkansas Razorbacks]].{{Citation | title = Kentucky's Woodson breaks record for passes without INT | year = 2007 | url = https://www.espn.com/espn/wire?section=ncf&id=3031824 | access-date = 2007-09-24}} The streak ended, however, when Woodson threw his first interception in 325 attempts on September 29, 2007, against [[Florida Atlantic University]].[https://web.archive.org/web/20241219022832/https://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=272720096 ESPN - Woodson throws career-high 5 TDs as No. 14 UK romps - NCAA College Football Recap] Against Florida State in the 2007 Music City Bowl, Woodson broke [[Danny Wuerffel]]'s SEC record for passing touchdowns in one season. Woodson threw 40 for the season, passing Wuerffel's record by one. '''Andre Dewayne Smith Jr.''' (born January 25, 1987) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Alabama Crimson Tide football|Alabama Crimson Tide]], earning [[unanimous All-American]] honors in 2008. He was selected by the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] in the first round of the [[2009 NFL draft]] with the sixth overall pick. He also played for the [[Minnesota Vikings]], [[Arizona Cardinals]], and [[Baltimore Ravens]].

==Early life==
Smith was born in [[Birmingham, Alabama]].  He attended [[Huffman High School]] in Birmingham, where he played football and competed in track. In [[high school football|football]], he was a three-year starter, a two-time All-State selection, and Class 6A Lineman of the Year in 2005. After registering 88 [[pancake blocks]] his senior season, Smith was selected "Mr. Football" by the Alabama Sports Writers Association, becoming the only offensive lineman to ever win the honor in the association's 23-year history. Smith earned High School All-American honors by ''[[USA Today]]'' and was selected to play in the 2006 [[U.S. Army All-American Bowl]]. He was also one of four finalists for the 2005 [[Walter Payton Trophy]], given to the nation's most athletic high school football player.

In addition to football, Smith also participated in [[track and field]] at Huffman. As a senior in 2006, Smith competed in the throwing events at the State Track & Field Meet, where he registered throws of 14.81 meters (48'7.25") in the [[shot put]] and 39.62 meters in the [[discus throw]] (126'8") that earned him sixth and eleventh-place finishes, respectively.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AHSAA - 2006 State Track & Field Meet Results - Class 6A Boys |url=https://dnn.ahsaa.com/Sports/IndividualSports/TrackField/History/StateTrackFieldResults/StateTrackField2006Results/2006StateTrackFieldMeetResultsClass6AB/tabid/2328/Default.aspx |access-date=2024-11-30 |website=AHSAA}}</ref>

|work=Scout.com |title=Andre Smith Recruiting Profile |url=http://recruiting.scout.com/a.z?s=73&p=8&c=1&nid=1528752 }}</ref> Smith was listed as the No. 1 offensive lineman by both recruiting services.<ref name="Rivals 2006 OG ranking">{{Cite web |work=Rivals.com |date=January 30, 2006 |title=Offensive guards 2006 |url=http://rivals100.rivals.com/viewrank.asp?ra_key=1151 }}</ref><ref |archive-date=February 13, 2007 }}</ref>

==College career==
Smith attended the [[University of Alabama]] beginning in 2006. In 2006, he played for Coach [[Mike Shula]] (and Coach [[Joe Kines]]).  In 2007 and 2008, he played for coach [[Nick Saban]]'s [[Alabama Crimson Tide football]] teams.  In his initial year at Alabama, he started all 13 games at left tackle, becoming only the fourth [[true freshman]] offensive lineman to start for the Crimson Tide.<ref>{{Cite news|date=August 30, 2006 |title=Notebooking the SEC Western Division |newspaper=The Sporting News |url=http://www.sportingnews.com/yourturn/viewtopic.php?t=122571 }}{{dead link|date=October 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Smith played at least 65 snaps in 10 of 13 games and played more than 70 snaps five times, while leading the Crimson Tide with 62 pancake blocks. He also scored a touchdown off of a lateral in the 34–31 [[2006 Independence Bowl|Independence Bowl]] loss against [[Oklahoma State Cowboys football|Oklahoma State]].<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=263620333| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190109155621/http://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=263620333| url-status=dead| archive-date=January 9, 2019| title=Ricks' field goal with 8.9 seconds left lifts Oklahoma State| agency=Associated Press| publisher=ESPN| date=December 28, 2006| access-date=April 26, 2009}}</ref> Smith earned Freshman All-American honors by the [[Football Writers Association of America]].<ref name="FWAA Freshmen">{{Cite web |last=Griffith |first=Mike |date=January 8, 2007 |title=Scripps/FWAA Freshman All-America Team |work=FWAA |url=http://www.sportswriters.net/fwaa/news/2006/allamerica070108.html }}</ref>

In [[2007 Alabama Crimson Tide football team|2007]], Smith was a first-team [[List of All-SEC football teams|All-Southeastern Conference]] selection, after starting every game at the left tackle position.<ref name="RollTide bio">{{cite web|url=http://www.rolltide.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/smith_andre00.html |title=Player Bio: Andre Smith |publisher=University of Alabama Athletics |access-date=April 26, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090418130959/http://www.rolltide.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/smith_andre00.html |archive-date=April 18, 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He was named Alabama Co-Player of the Week four times during the season.<ref name="RollTide bio" />

Smith was recognized as a unanimous All-American in [[2008 College Football All-America Team|2008]], as well as the 2008 [[Outland Trophy]] winner. He was also considered to be one of the best underclassmen for the [[2009 NFL draft]].<ref>{{cite web| url=http://walterfootball.com/draft2009OT.php| title=2009 NFL Draft: Offensive Tackle Rankings| publisher=WalterFootball.com| date=November 1, 2008| access-date=December 5, 2008| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20081206080240/http://walterfootball.com/draft2009OT.php| archive-date= December 6, 2008 | url-status= live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=https://insider.espn.com/nfl/draft09/insider/columns/story?columnist=mcshay_todd&id=3566482| title=Linemen, linebackers dominate Scouts Inc.'s top 32 senior prospects| publisher=Scouts Inc| last=McShay| first=Todd| date=September 3, 2008| access-date=December 5, 2008}}</ref> He was also a first-team All-SEC selection and shared the league's [[Jacobs Blocking Trophy]] with Arkansas center Jonathan Luigs.<ref>{{cite news| title=Reaching His Goals, Alabama's Smith Already Distinguished SEC Lineman| work=Columbus Ledger-Enquirer| pages=B7| date=December 14, 2007}}</ref> He led the team with 103 key knockdowns and added seven blocks downfield. He was penalized just twice and he allowed just one QB sack and six pressures on 334 pass plays.<ref name="RollTide bio" />

==Professional career==

===Pre-draft===
Widely believed to be the best run-blocking tackle in the [[2009 NFL draft]], Smith drew comparisons to [[Jason Peters]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 25, 2009 |publisher=SportingNews.com |title=Pro Football War Room: Amdre Smith |url=http://warroom.sportingnews.com/nfl/draft/2009/players/8379.html }}</ref> At the 2009 [[NFL Combine]], Smith weighed 332 pounds.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://blogs.usatoday.com/thehuddle/2009/02/alabamas-smith.html |title=Alabama's Smith sorry after going AWOL from combine |work=USA Today |date=February 21, 2009 |access-date=April 25, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090225121226/http://blogs.usatoday.com/thehuddle/2009/02/alabamas-smith.html |archive-date=February 25, 2009 }}</ref> He also looked out of shape as he ran 40 yards shirtless, clocking at a slow 5.28, and had a disappointing 19 repetitions on the bench with 225 pounds.<ref name="Cooney USA Today">{{Cite news |last=Cooney |first=Frank |date=March 29, 2009 |title=Peak performers: O-line likely to produce bumper draft class again |newspaper=USA Today |url=https://www.usatoday.com/sports/football/nfl/2009-03-29-sw-offensive-line_N.htm }}</ref>

He decided to leave the combine early in order to prepare for Alabama's Pro Day on March 11, 2009. Smith, however, did not inform his group leader at the combine before he left, and later apologized, stating: "If I had the chance to do it all over, I wouldn't have handled it the way I did. I should have told my group leader that I was leaving, and I didn't. I didn't mean to ruffle any feathers or step on any toes. I didn't mean to grandstand anyone at the combine. That was not my intention at all, and I apologize for my mistake." Smith also admitted that he wasn't prepared or in shape.<ref name="Smith-bails-combine" /><ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2009-feb-22-sp-nfl-combine22-story.html| title=Tackle Andre Smith leaves without notice| author=Farmer, Sam| work=Los Angeles Times| date=February 22, 2009| access-date=April 25, 2009}}</ref>

His Pro Day performance at Alabama on March 11, 2009, was equally unimpressive, although his weight was down to 325 pounds.
